summary.text: For an odd prime \(p\) properly dividing \(n\), with \(t=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\), LTE assigns every \(p\)-adic contribution from a multiple \(pj\) in \((n-1)!\) to the distinct factor \(2^{tj}-1\), while the omitted multiple \(n\) yields one surplus \(p\)-factor; hence \(p\mid a(n-1)\), contradicting the assumed divisibility since \(p\nmid 2\). Thus a composite \(n\) would be \(2^r\), ruled out by \(v_2(a(2^r-1))=r-1\), and if a prime \(p\) had \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<p-1\), the factor \(2^{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)}-1\) similarly gives \(p\mid a(p-1)\), again forcing the impossible divisibility \(p\mid 2^{p-2}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 P_m=\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1),\qquad
 N_m=2^{m-1}P_m \quad (m\geq 1).
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
 a(m)=\frac{N_m}{m!}
      =\frac{2^{m-1}}{m!}\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1).
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and establish two stronger divisibility facts about it.

For a prime \(q\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in a positive integer \(x\). We repeatedly use the following standard odd-prime lifting-the-exponent formula. If \(q\) is odd, \(q\mid x-y\), and \(q\nmid xy\), then, for every positive integer \(j\),
\[
 v_q(x^j-y^j)=v_q(x-y)+v_q(j).
\]
In particular, if \(t>0\) and \(q\mid 2^t-1\), then
\[
 v_q(2^{tj}-1)=v_q(2^t-1)+v_q(j)\geq 1+v_q(j)=v_q(qj). \tag{1}
\]

We also use elementary facts about multiplicative order. For an odd prime \(q\), let
\[
 t=\operatorname{ord}_q(2).
\]
Since \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(q\), Fermat's theorem gives \(2^{q-1}\equiv1\pmod q\). Hence
\[
 1\leq t\leq q-1,\qquad t\mid q-1,\qquad q\mid 2^t-1. \tag{2}
\]

### 1. Integrality of the formula for \(a(m)\)

We first prove that, for every positive \(m\),
\[
 m!\mid 2^{m-1}P_m. \tag{3}
\]
It is enough to compare the valuations at every prime divisor \(q\) of \(m!\).

Suppose first that \(q\) is odd, and let \(t=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)\). Consider all multiples of \(q\) in \(\{1,2,\ldots,m\}\). Write each such multiple as \(i=qj\), and associate to it the index
\[
 f(i)=tj.
\]
This index belongs to \(\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\): it is positive, and by (2),
\[
 tj\leq(q-1)j<qj=i\leq m.
\]
The association is injective because \(t>0\). Moreover, by (1),
\[
 v_q(i)=v_q(qj)\leq v_q(2^{tj}-1)=v_q(2^{f(i)}-1).
\]
Only multiples of \(q\) contribute to \(v_q(m!)\). Summing the preceding inequalities over those multiples, and then observing that the resulting factors are distinct factors among those forming \(P_m\), gives
\[
 v_q(m!)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_q(i)
 \leq \sum_{k=1}^{m-1}v_q(2^k-1)=v_q(P_m). \tag{4}
\]

For \(q=2\), every factor \(2^k-1\) is odd, but the initial power of two supplies the needed valuation. Indeed, by Legendre's formula,
\[
 v_2(m!)=\sum_{s\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{2^s}\right\rfloor<m,
\]
so, being an integer, \(v_2(m!)\leq m-1=v_2(2^{m-1})\). Together with (4), this proves (3). Therefore the displayed quotient defining \(a(m)\) is exact in the integers.

### 2. A proper odd prime divisor of \(n\) divides \(a(n-1)\)

We need a strengthening of (4). Let \(p\) be an odd prime such that
\[
 p\mid n,\qquad p<n.
\]
We claim that
\[
 p\mid a(n-1). \tag{5}
\]
Put \(m=n-1\), let \(t=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\), and write
\[
 j_0=\frac np.
\]
Because \(p<n\), we have \(j_0\geq2\).

As in the integrality proof, associate to every multiple \(i=pj\) in \(\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) the index \(tj\). These indices are distinct and lie in \(\{1,\ldots,n-2\}\), and (1) shows that the associated factors \(2^{tj}-1\) collectively contain at least all the copies of \(p\) occurring in \((n-1)!\).

There is now one additional index, corresponding to the next multiple \(n=pj_0\), namely
\[
 k_0=tj_0.
\]
It too lies in \(\{1,\ldots,n-2\}\). Indeed, it is positive, and
\[
 k_0=tj_0\leq(p-1)j_0=pj_0-j_0=n-j_0\leq n-2.
\]
It is not one of the indices already used: equality \(tj=tj_0\) would imply \(j=j_0\), hence \(i=pj=n\), whereas the previously used multiples satisfy \(i\leq n-1\). Finally, (1), applied to \(j_0\), shows in particular that
\[
 v_p(2^{k_0}-1)\geq v_p(pj_0)=v_p(n)\geq1.
\]
Consequently the product in the numerator of \(a(n-1)\) has at least one more factor of \(p\) than the denominator:
\[
 v_p\!\left(\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1)\right)
 \geq v_p((n-1)!)+1. \tag{6}
\]
Since the division by \((n-1)!\) is exact, valuations subtract. The power \(2^{n-2}\) in the numerator contributes no negative valuation, so (6) implies
\[
 v_p(a(n-1))\geq1,
\]
which proves (5).

### 3. The special case where \(n\) is a power of two

We next calculate exactly the power of two dividing \(a(2^r-1)\). For every \(r>0\),
\[
 v_2\bigl(a(2^r-1)\bigr)=r-1. \tag{7}
\]
To see this, put \(m=2^r-1\). Every factor \(2^k-1\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2(N_m)=v_2(2^{m-1})=m-1.
\]
Legendre's formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_2(m!)
 &=\sum_{s=1}^{r-1}\left\lfloor\frac{2^r-1}{2^s}\right\rfloor\\
 &=\sum_{s=1}^{r-1}(2^{r-s}-1)
 =2^r-1-r
 =m-r.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(m!\mid N_m\), subtraction of valuations yields
\[
 v_2(a(m))=(m-1)-(m-r)=r-1,
\]
which is (7).

It follows that for every \(r\geq2\),
\[
 2^r\nmid a(2^r-1)+2^{2^r-2}. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, the elementary inequality
\[
 r\leq 2^r-2 \qquad(r\geq2)
\]
shows that \(2^r\mid 2^{2^r-2}\). If \(2^r\) also divided the sum in (8), subtracting this second summand would imply \(2^r\mid a(2^r-1)\), contrary to (7), which says that the exact exponent of \(2\) in that number is only \(r-1\).

### 4. The hypothesis forces \(n\) to be prime

Now suppose \(n>2\) and
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{9}
\]
Assume for contradiction that \(n\) is composite.

First suppose that \(n\) has an odd prime divisor \(q\). Since \(n\) is composite, this prime divisor is proper: \(q<n\). By (5),
\[
 q\mid a(n-1).
\]
Also \(q\mid n\), so (9) implies
\[
 q\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Subtracting gives \(q\mid2^{n-2}\). A prime dividing a power of \(2\) must divide \(2\), so \(q=2\), contradicting that \(q\) is odd.

It remains to consider the case in which \(n\) has no odd prime divisor. By unique factorization, all prime factors of \(n\) are then \(2\), and hence
\[
 n=2^r
\]
for some integer \(r\geq0\). Since \(n>2\), necessarily \(r\geq2\). Substitution into (9) gives
\[
 2^r\mid a(2^r-1)+2^{2^r-2},
\]
which contradicts (8). Thus no composite \(n\) can satisfy (9), and therefore \(n\) is prime.

### 5. For this prime, \(2\) must be a primitive root

It remains to prove that \(2\) has multiplicative order \(n-1=\varphi(n)\) modulo the now-known prime \(n\).

We first establish the relevant auxiliary fact. Let \(p>2\) be prime. If \(2\) is not a primitive root modulo \(p\), then
\[
 p\mid a(p-1). \tag{10}
\]
Let \(t=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\). Fermat's theorem gives \(t\mid p-1\). Failure of \(2\) to be a primitive root means \(t\ne p-1\); hence
\[
 1\leq t<p-1,
\]
so in fact \(1\leq t\leq p-2\). Therefore the factor \(2^t-1\) occurs in
\[
 \prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1),
\]
and by the definition of order it is divisible by \(p\). On the other hand, \(p\nmid(p-1)!\), because every factor in \((p-1)!\) is smaller than \(p\). Thus the numerator in
\[
 a(p-1)=\frac{2^{p-2}\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1)}{(p-1)!}
\]
has positive \(p\)-adic valuation while the denominator has valuation zero. Since the quotient is exact, the factor of \(p\) remains in the quotient. This proves (10).

Apply this with \(p=n\). If \(2\) were not a primitive root modulo \(n\), (10) would give
\[
 n\mid a(n-1).
\]
Together with (9), subtraction would yield
\[
 n\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
Since \(n\) is prime, this would imply \(n\mid2\). But \(n>2\), which is impossible.

Hence \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\). Since \(n\) is prime, \(\varphi(n)=n-1\), so equivalently the residue class of \(2\) modulo \(n\) has multiplicative order \(\varphi(n)\). We have proved both required conclusions: \(n\) is prime and \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).
